newsitem.title: USA: FAA said to refuse to release airline safety rankings.
newsitem.headline: FAA said to refuse to release airline safety rankings.

text.p: A former senior official of the Transportation Department said on Tuesday the Federal Aviation Administraton had accident and incident ratings for U.S. airlines but refused to make them public.

Mary Schaivo said at a news conference and in a recently published book, "Flying Blind, Flying Safe," that the FAA knew airlines did not want the information made public "and what the aviation industry wants, the FAA wants too."
"They have it, and they even use it to target and track airlines," said Schaivo, who was Inspector General at the Transportation Department from 1990-96.

She said that the FAA released raw data about accidents and incidents, but not its airline ratings. "In the limited comparative safety information it does routinely release, it deletes the name of the airline and all identifying information," Schiavo added.
But FAA spokesman Eliot Brenner said flatly: "The FAA does not rank airlines as to safety."
He said that to lump together accidents, which would include a crash, and incidents, which would include an ankle sprained in turbulence, would make it a meaningless exercise.

Schiavo said she used FAA data to rank airlines and it showed that from 1991-95, Continental Airlines Inc., Delta Air Lines Inc., and American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp, had the highest accident/incident rates per 100,000 takeoffs.
Southwest Airlines Co. had the lowest, she said.

Schiavo said America West Holdings Corp. showed the most near misses in the air and Trans World Airlines Inc. the fewest. American had the most pilot deviations from prescribed procedures, for weather, mechanical or other reason, and America West the fewest.
She also said the FAA had put a monetary value of $2.7 million on a human life, and this was used in cost-benefit assessments of whether to require safety modifications.

Schiavo said the National Transportation Safety Board had repeatedly urged that smoke detectors be required in cargo holds, but the FAA rejected the idea, saying that its $350 million cost was too much for the industry.
But then, she said, ValuJet Inc. flight 592 crashed near Miami last May 11, killing all 110 people on board, with a fire in the hold cited as the tentative cause.
"If the FAA places a value on human life as rumors have told me -- somewhere around $2.7 million -- then the ValuJet crash sadly gave them their dollar value, their body count." she said.
"We had to quesion who the FAA was serving," she said.
FAA officials said the figure was not new nor was the idea that changes to planes be considered on a cost-benefit basis. Other agencies also base changes on cost effectiveness, they said.
Schiavo criticized what she called the FAA's lack of attention to recommendations by the NTSB, the agency mandated to probe aviation accidents and to recommend safety improvements.
"We need the NTSB to have more authority to make and enforce the changes that literally save people's lives," she said.

The FAA, asked about Schiavo's comments, repeated its comments that America's aviation system was the safest in the world, carrying 1.6 billion passengers safely every day. It said it would spend $4.4 billion this year on air safety.
